# Context Engineering {#sec-context-engineering}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements run `qwen3.5:9b` through
`ollama` 0.24.0 on invented facts embedded in real Turkish news articles, so a
correct answer can only have come from the context. This chapter is the
consequence of @sec-agent-anatomy's finding that the transcript *is* the
agent's state; @sec-memory covers what persists between runs. One reproduction
note if you rerun the long-context probe: `ollama` silently truncates a prompt
longer than the served `num_ctx` (its context-length setting) and warns about
nothing. Set it explicitly above your longest condition, and check the served
length rather than assuming it. An 11k-token prompt quietly cut to 4k is no
longer a long-context condition, and the cut may remove a needle as well, so
neither a flat curve nor a drop would mean what it seems to. Software: NumPy
2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- treat the context window as a budget with a measurable return rather than a
  container with a capacity;
- measure degradation on your own task instead of assuming either that a big
  window is free or that it is ruinous;
- apply compaction, isolation and just-in-time retrieval deliberately, knowing
  what each one costs;
- cut an agent's token usage substantially without losing accuracy.

## A budget, not a container {#sec-context-engineering-budget}

The window is usually described as a capacity: *200k tokens, so you can fit
200k tokens*. That framing is wrong in a way that matters, because it suggests
the only question is whether things fit.

Three results from earlier chapters say otherwise, and together they make the
case for treating the window as a budget where **every token competes**:

- @sec-rag measured the price of not choosing: eighty documents instead of the
  one that mattered cost **148× the input tokens for identical accuracy**. The
  model was not confused by the extra material. You simply paid for it, on
  every request, forever.
- @sec-agent-anatomy showed that in an agent the context is not something you
  compose once — the transcript *is* the state, it only grows, and every model
  call re-sends all of it.
- @sec-tool-design showed that a tool's return value is therefore a **write to
  that state**, which is why a tool returning 50,000 tokens can take space its
  later steps need, and is carried into every later call.

[So there are two questions, not one: "does it fit" — capacity is a real
constraint — and, for everything that does, "what is each token
earning".]{.hl} The second is the one nobody asks.

That reframing has an immediate practical consequence: you cannot answer the
second question without instrumentation. The first move in context engineering
is not a technique, it is a **budget by category** — how many tokens went to
the system prompt, to tool definitions, to retrieved documents, to
observations, to history. Almost everyone who runs that count for the first
time finds one category they did not know was there and would not have guessed.

::: {.column-margin}
The categories that surprise people, in rough order of frequency: tool
definitions, which are re-sent on every call and scale with the number of
tools; a system prompt that accumulated instructions nobody has read in
months; and retrieved documents whose *k* was set once and never revisited.
None of these are visible without counting.
:::

### The one thing that changes the arithmetic {#sec-context-engineering-cache}

One qualifier before any of that arithmetic gets applied. Providers cache the
**prefix** of a prompt: an unchanged system prompt and tool block, re-sent on
the next call, is billed at a fraction of its first-call price and skips most
of the *prefill* (the pass that reads the prompt before the first output token)
— @sec-serving measured warm prefill flat at 12–16 ms whatever the prompt
length. So "every token is re-sent on every call" is exactly true of the
*tokens* and only partly true of the bill.

Why only a *prefix*? Because attention is causal: the keys and values stored
for token *i* (the KV cache of @sec-attention-cost) depend on every token
before it. Change one token and everything after it has to be recomputed,
while everything before it can be reused. The practical rules follow from
that one fact (@sec-serving-cache has the mechanics). The prefix must be
byte-identical, so a timestamp or a user name near the top of the system
prompt quietly switches caching off for everything below it. By default a
cache entry also expires after a few idle minutes, and some providers charge a
premium to write it.

A worked example makes the size of the effect concrete. Take a 10-call agent
run whose system prompt and tool definitions total 5,000 tokens, and use
multipliers that are typical of 2026 price sheets (they vary by provider and
model): a cache write costs 1.25× the normal input price, a cache read 0.1×.
Uncached, the fixed part costs what 10 × 5,000 = 50,000 input tokens cost.
Cached, it costs what 1.25 × 5,000 + 9 × 0.1 × 5,000 = 10,750 cost — about
4.7 times less, for exactly the same tokens.

Two consequences follow, and both make cutting tokens worth less than the raw
count suggests. Fixed costs are cheaper than they look, so pruning the system
prompt returns less than multiplying it by the step count suggests. And
**compaction invalidates the cache**: rewriting the middle of a context
invalidates the cached prefix from that point on, so the first call after you
compact pays full price — plus any write premium — for everything after the
rewritten point. Design the context to be append-only where you can — stable
prefix, growing suffix, the task restated at the end — and compact rarely in
large steps rather than often in small ones.

**What we will look at.** First whether long contexts really do degrade, where
this chapter's own measurement finds nothing and the published benchmarks find
a collapse — and the reason for the disagreement is the most useful thing in
the section. Then the four techniques: compaction, which is a lossy
compression problem where you choose the loss in advance; isolation, which is
usually the largest single lever; just-in-time retrieval
instead of loading everything up front; and the filesystem as somewhere to put
what the transcript cannot hold. And finally the case where all of it still
fails, because the data was never text.

## Does a long context actually degrade? {#sec-context-engineering-rot}

The budget argument above is about money. There is a second, louder claim —
that long contexts degrade *accuracy* — and it deserves separating from the
first, because the two lead to different engineering.

@sec-rag tested it and found nothing: 640 queries, sixteen conditions, up to
16,775 tokens, **100% at every context size and every position**. I ran a
harder local version for this chapter — two invented figures to find and add
rather than one to locate — and the curve was still essentially flat:

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 60 tasks, two invented figures to find and sum

 distractor docs  accuracy   95% CI          prompt tokens
               0    100.0%   [94.0, 100.0]             142
               4     93.3%   [84.1,  97.4]             863
              12     88.3%   [77.8,  94.2]           2,319
              28     88.3%   [77.8,  94.2]           5,228
              60     96.7%   [88.6,  99.1]          11,048
```

Sixty distractors scored *higher* than twelve. That non-monotone shape is
consistent with noise, but it does not establish it — a real effect of content
or position need not be monotone either. The intervals
overlap heavily — but overlapping intervals are not a test, so here is one.
The largest gap, 0 against 12 distractors (60/60 versus 53/60), sits on the
same 60 tasks, so the right instrument is the paired one: all seven
disagreements run the same way, and exact McNemar gives a two-sided
$p = 2 \times 2^{-7} = 0.0156$. (Fisher's exact test, which treats the two
conditions as independent samples, gives 0.013 — close here, and the wrong
model of the data.) Across four comparisons the Bonferroni line is 0.0125, so
it fails either way and I will not claim it. The comparison the
headline rests on, 0 against 60 distractors, gives p = 0.50. So: adding 78×
the tokens made no difference this sample can detect — which is not evidence
that the conditions are equivalent — and the dip in the middle sits right at
the edge of what 60 tasks can resolve either way.

### Why the easy test finds nothing

The name for the louder claim is *context rot*: a model's accuracy decays as
its input grows, even when everything still fits in the window. It would be
comfortable to conclude that context rot is folklore. It is not.
@hong2025contextrot, the report that popularised the name, ran 18 frontier
models on deliberately simple tasks at lengths inside their advertised windows,
and found performance degrading as the input grew in every one of its
experiments. My two experiments missed it for two reasons rather than one.

The simpler reason first: 11,048 tokens is about a third of the length at
which the published benchmarks report their headline drops, so this probe
never entered the regime they measure. The second reason is the interesting
one, because it is the same reason most in-house evaluations miss the effect
even when they *do* reach the length.

**Both of my tests allowed literal matching.** Both were
*needle-in-a-haystack* (NIAH) tests: one fact — the *needle* — is hidden in a
long filler text — the *haystack* — and the model is asked for it. The
question contained `ZRG-14`; so did the needle. Attention is extremely good at finding a rare
string that is already in the query. @modarressi2025nolima was built exactly
to remove that crutch — its needles share minimal lexical overlap with the
question, so the model has to infer the association rather than match it — and
the result is stark: across **13 models that all claim 128K contexts, 11 fall
below half their short-context baseline at 32K tokens**. Even GPT-4o, one of
the two exceptions that stayed above half, goes from **99.3% to 69.7%**.

@hsieh2024ruler reaches the same place from a different direction, and states
the trap plainly: models show near-perfect scores on vanilla
needle-in-a-haystack, yet on a benchmark that extends the test beyond search —
to multi-hop tracing and aggregation — **almost all of them show large drops as
the context grows**. Across 17 models claiming 32K or more,
only half maintain satisfactory performance at 32K.

So the honest synthesis, which is more useful than either result alone:

| what you measure | what you will find |
|:--|:--|
| Locating a rare string that appears in the query | little or no degradation at the lengths tested here; this is what my tests and vanilla NIAH measure |
| Locating information by *meaning*, not by string match | progressive degradation, largest where it was measured: 11 of 13 models below half their short-context baseline **by** 32K, not starting there [@modarressi2025nolima] |
| Tracing across several facts, or aggregating them | large degradation, earlier [@hsieh2024ruler] |

: Three tasks, three different answers about the same window {tbl-colwidths="[46,54]"}

[A model's advertised context length is a capacity, not a competence]{.hl} —
its [**effective context length**](#gloss-effective-context-length){#term-effective-context-length .term-ref}
is an empirical quantity and usually much shorter.

::: {#gloss-effective-context-length .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Effective context length** — the length at which a model still performs, as
opposed to the length it accepts. Routinely far shorter than the advertised
window. [↩](#term-effective-context-length){.term-back}
:::

**Why this might happen, mechanically.** Two mechanisms are usually offered,
and they are plausible rather than established — nothing below is measured in
this chapter. Attention weights are a softmax over every key in the context, so
adding keys gives the mass somewhere else to go — *dilution*. Note this is a
tendency and not an identity: the scores are not fixed while the denominator
grows, and a model that learns to score the relevant token higher in a longer
context can hold or increase its share. A
literal string match plausibly holds up better because it produces one large
score where a semantic association produces several medium ones — but even a
large score is diluted: with a target logit $a$ and $N$ equal distractor logits
$b$, the target's weight is $e^{a}/(e^{a} + N e^{b})$, which still falls as $N$
grows for any finite gap. Treat this as a possible mechanism, unmeasured
here.
Separately, many advertised windows are only partly *trained* windows. A model
pretrained at 8K is typically extended to 128K by rescaling its RoPE positions
(Position Interpolation, YaRN — @sec-position) plus a comparatively short
continued training on long inputs. It works, but the model has seen far fewer
examples of long distances than of short ones, and quality tends to fall with
distance. That is the likely machinery behind *capacity, not competence*.

One published result points the other way and is worth holding onto.
@shi2023large found that irrelevant sentences added to arithmetic word
problems dropped accuracy substantially, with no length increase to blame. My
distractors cost nothing and theirs cost a great deal — the difference is the
task. Distractors are cheap when the job is to *find* a literal string and
expensive when the job is to *reason*, because reasoning has to decide what is
relevant and literal matching does not.

And the widely-run test that would reassure you — needle-in-a-haystack — is
precisely the test that its built-in lexical overlap makes easy. If you take one
operational thing from this section, make it this: **evaluate long context on
your own task with your own paraphrases, never on literal matches**, because
the literal-match version will pass and tell you nothing.

::: {.column-margin}
Which is @sec-rag's lesson restated in a place where it costs real money: a
test that everything passes is not a test. My local experiment is small — one
9B model, 60 tasks, up to 11k tokens — and it agrees with the published
result *about the easy case*, which is the most it can establish. The
published benchmarks are the evidence for the hard case, and they were run at
a scale no laptop reaches.
:::

## Compaction: what to keep, summarise, and drop {#sec-context-engineering-compaction}

@sec-agent-anatomy established that the transcript only grows.
[**Compaction**](#gloss-compaction){#term-compaction .term-ref} is what you do
about that, and it is a lossy compression problem with an unusual property:
**you choose what to lose, and you choose it before you know what will be
needed.**

::: {#gloss-compaction .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Compaction** — summarising or dropping parts of an agent's transcript so the
context stops growing. Lossy, and the loss is chosen before you know what will
be needed. [↩](#term-compaction){.term-back}
:::

The useful move is to stop treating the transcript as one thing. It has parts
with very different value per token:

| part of the transcript | keep it how | why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| The **task** — what the user actually asked | verbatim, always, and re-state it near the end | it is short, it is the thing being optimised against, and it is what gets lost when history dominates |
| **Decisions** the agent made and their reasons | summarised | *what* was decided is needed; the deliberation that produced it usually is not |
| **Tool results** that are still live | verbatim | these are facts the answer depends on. Summarising a number is how you lose it |
| **Tool results** already superseded or consumed | drop, or reduce to one line | the ten search results you rejected are pure cost from the moment you rejected them |
| **Errors** already recovered from | drop the traceback, keep one line of what it taught | @sec-agent-anatomy's point: a stale error keeps conditioning the model toward the confusion it caused — but "the date field wants ISO-8601" is the sentence that stops it happening again, and it costs eight tokens |

: Not all tokens are worth the same {tbl-colwidths="[26,18,56]"}

Three failure modes are worth knowing before you build this.

**Summarising numbers.** A summariser will happily turn *the budget is 4,318
lira* into *the budget was discussed*. Any value the final answer must contain
should be exempt from compaction by rule, not by hope — the safest
implementation keeps a structured `facts` list beside the prose and never
summarises it.

**Compacting the task away.** As history grows, the original request drifts
toward the middle of a long context. @liu2024lost measured what that costs:
accuracy on a retrieval task is highest when the relevant material sits at the
beginning or the end of the input and degrades markedly in the middle. My own
needle test did *not* reproduce this — 100% at every position — for the same
reason it found nothing else: a literal string match is immune to where it
sits. Re-stating the objective at the end of the context is nearly free — the
task is short, and appending it leaves the cached prefix intact — and it largely
stops the task getting lost in the middle. It does not fix *evidence* that sits
there; the remedy for that is the selecting and cutting the rest of this chapter
is about.

**Compaction that is not idempotent.** Summarising a summary loses more each
time, and long-running agents do this repeatedly. Compact from the *original*
where you can, or accept and measure the drift.

### Rolling history, concretely

The pattern that works in practice is a three-tier window:

```text
  [ system prompt + tools ]     fixed, always present
  [ compacted history      ]    everything older than the last N steps,
                                summarised once, with a facts list kept verbatim
  [ last N steps           ]    verbatim, because recent detail is what the
                                next decision is actually about
  [ the task, restated     ]    last, so it is never in the middle
```

Choosing N is an empirical question with a cheap answer: run your eval at
N = 3, 5 and 10 and take the smallest that does not lose accuracy.

## Isolation: give the specialist a clean window {#sec-context-engineering-isolation}

Compaction reduces a context you have already polluted.
[**Context isolation**](#gloss-context-isolation){#term-context-isolation .term-ref}
avoids polluting it.

::: {#gloss-context-isolation .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Context isolation** — running a read-heavy sub-task in its own window and
returning only its conclusion, so the parent's context never carries what it
read. The reading is still paid for, once, by the sub-agent.
[↩](#term-context-isolation){.term-back}
:::

The idea is simple and it is the single largest lever in this chapter: a
sub-task that needs to read a great deal — search fifty documents, scan a log,
try six queries — runs in **its own context**, and returns only its
conclusion. The parent never sees the fifty documents. It sees one paragraph.

```text
  without isolation           with isolation
  ─────────────────           ──────────────
  parent reads 50 docs        sub-agent reads 50 docs in a fresh window
  parent context: 40k         sub-agent returns 200 tokens
  and stays 40k forever       parent context: +200
```

The saving is not the 40k. On the parent's side it is roughly
$(40{,}000 - 200) \times M$ **over the $M$ model calls left in its loop**. That
is a gross figure. The sub-agent's own 40k of reading, its fixed prompt and
output, and any cache pricing still have to be subtracted, so treat the sketch
as illustrative rather than as a bill. How large $M$ is depends on
something @sec-agent-anatomy measured rather than assumed. When the steps are
independent the model batches its tool calls: five lookups collapsed into 2.0
model calls there, and the growth was nowhere near quadratic. When the steps
are genuinely sequential — step *n* needs step *n*−1's result — the multiplier
is the step count and the isolation saving is at its largest. Isolation pays
most exactly where batching cannot help.

What it costs is equally real and usually understated:

- **The parent cannot see what the sub-agent saw.** If the returned paragraph
  is wrong or incomplete, the parent has no way to notice — it has lost the
  evidence. Return a short result *and* a pointer to where the full material
  lives.
- **Coordination is not free.** Every isolated call is at least one extra
  round trip, and the specialist has to be given enough context to do its job,
  which is a prompt you now maintain.
- **Errors compound quietly.** A summary that is 90% right, consumed by a
  parent that treats it as fact, is a failure mode with no error message.
  @sec-multi-agent is where this gets its own chapter.

The heuristic worth applying: **isolate when the sub-task's inputs are large
and its output is small.** Searching, scanning, filtering, verifying. Do not
isolate when the parent will need the detail — you will only pay the round
trip and then ask for it again.

## Just-in-time retrieval beats eager loading {#sec-context-engineering-jit}

The instinct when building an agent is to load what it might need: the schema,
the docs, the recent tickets, the user's history. It is one fewer failure
mode, and it feels like preparation.

It is also paying for everything on every call. The alternative — give the
agent the *ability* to fetch and let it fetch what it needs — is almost always
cheaper, and @sec-rag's measurement is the reason to believe it: eighty
documents instead of one cost 148× the input for identical accuracy. Eager
loading is that trade, made silently, on every request.

Two things make just-in-time work, and both are @sec-tool-design's subject:

- **The agent has to know what is available.** A tool named `find_orders` with
  a description saying when it applies is what makes fetching-on-demand
  possible at all. This is why the two chapters are adjacent.
- **Identifiers beat payloads.** Pass around order IDs, file paths and URLs;
  fetch the contents when needed. A pointer costs ten tokens and a document
  costs two thousand, and most pointers are never dereferenced.

What it costs is **latency**: a round trip you would not have paid, on the
steps that need the data. That is a real trade and it has an obvious middle
ground — eagerly load the one or two things needed on nearly every request,
fetch everything else on demand. What makes it a decision rather than a habit
is measuring the hit rate: if you eagerly load something that is used 15% of
the time, you are paying for it 85% of the time for nothing.

## The filesystem as external memory {#sec-context-engineering-filesystem}

There is a move that sounds like a workaround and is closer to the right
architecture: **let the agent write things down and read them back.**

A scratchpad file, a notes directory, a structured JSON of findings so far.
The context holds a *reference* — `findings.md`, 340 lines — and the agent
reads the part it needs when it needs it.

This is better than a longer window for reasons that have nothing to do with
capacity:

- **It survives compaction.** Anything written to a file is still there after
  the transcript is summarised, which makes it the natural home for exactly
  the facts that compaction destroys.
- **It is addressable.** The agent can re-read one section rather than
  re-reading everything, which a linear transcript cannot offer.
- **It is inspectable by you.** A file is a debugging artefact and a
  transcript is a haystack. When a long run goes wrong, the notes file is
  usually where you find out why.
- **It survives the run.** Which is where this chapter hands over to
  @sec-memory, whose subject is what should persist *between* runs rather than
  within one.

The discipline that makes it work: **write structured, read selectively.** A
notes file that becomes free-form prose is a second transcript with the same
problem. Give it headings, or make it JSON, so a later step can read one field
rather than the whole file.

## When text retrieval is not enough {#sec-context-engineering-structure}

One caveat on everything above, because it is where a well-built context
pipeline still fails.

@sec-rag's machinery — chunk, embed, retrieve — assumes the information is
*text with local meaning*: a passage that means roughly the same thing on its
own as it did in the document. Three common cases break that assumption
outright, and no amount of chunking repairs them:

- **Tables and schemas.** A row is meaningless without its header, and a
  column name is meaningless without the table's purpose. @sec-rag measured
  what chunking does to structure; the fix here is not better chunking but
  serialising each row into a self-contained sentence, or not retrieving at
  all and letting the agent query the table.
- **Code.** A function's meaning depends on its callers, its types and the
  module's conventions — all of which live elsewhere in the repository.
  Retrieving the function body alone retrieves the least useful part.
- **Anything relational.** *Which customers churned after the March incident*
  is a join, not a search. Embedding rows and hoping is the expensive way to
  get a worse answer than a query would have given.

The rule: **when the data has structure, give the agent a way to query the
structure.** For the query shapes above — aggregates, joins, follow the callers
of this function — a `run_sql` tool over a real schema beats embedding rows,
and a `grep`-and-`read` pair beats embedding a codebase. It is a claim about
those query shapes, not a general ranking: a question like *where do we handle
retries* has no exact string to grep for, and that is what embedding search is
good at. Most real systems want both. That is a
context-engineering decision, because it determines what ends up in the window
— and it is usually the difference between an agent that works on your data
and one that works on a demo.

## Intuition checks {#sec-context-engineering-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. Two rest on measurements — one published,
one run here — and the other four on judgements this chapter argues for and
tells you how to check on your own system.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your model has a 200K window. Can you stop thinking about context?

No, for two separate reasons that are easy to conflate. The **cost** reason is
close to unconditional: every token is re-sent on every model call, so a
context you did not curate is a bill you pay forever — @sec-rag measured 148×
the input for identical accuracy. Prompt caching discounts the part of the
prefix that does not change, which is why the part that *does* change is where
the money is. The **capability** reason is conditional but real: a
window is a capacity, not a competence, and @hsieh2024ruler found that of 17
models claiming 32K or more, only half held up at 32K.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. You ran needle-in-a-haystack and scored 100%. What have you learned?

Almost nothing about your task. NIAH lets the model match a rare string that
is already in the question, which is the easiest thing attention does —
@sec-rag's run returned a flat 100% at every size and position, and this
chapter's harder local version stayed between 88.3% and 100% with no trend in
context length.
@modarressi2025nolima removed exactly that crutch and **11 of 13 models fell
below half their short-context baseline at 32K**; even GPT-4o, one of the
exceptions, went from 99.3% to 69.7%. Test with paraphrases, not literal matches.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. What is the first thing to do when an agent costs too much?

Count, by category — system prompt, tool definitions, retrieved documents,
tool results, history. Not because counting is virtuous but because the
largest category is routinely not the one people assume. The fixed costs
(system prompt, tool definitions) are multiplied by every step in the loop, so
their token count is larger than it looks — but a cached prefix bills those
repeats at a discount, so rank categories by measured cost, not by tokens
alone.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. When should a sub-task get its own context?

When its inputs are large and its output is small: searching, scanning,
filtering, verifying. The saving is not the tokens the sub-task read, it is
those tokens multiplied by every remaining model call in the parent's loop —
minus what the sub-agent itself costs.
Do not isolate when the parent will need the detail — you pay a round trip and
then ask for it again. And return a pointer alongside the summary, because the
parent has otherwise lost the evidence and cannot notice a wrong conclusion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. What must never be summarised?

Numbers, identifiers, and anything the final answer has to contain. A
summariser will turn *the budget is 4,318 lira* into *the budget was
discussed* without any signal that it did. Keep a structured facts list beside
the prose and exempt it from compaction by rule. Also worth protecting: the
original task, restated at the end of the context rather than left to drift
into the middle.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your agent works on your demo data and fails on the real database. Why?

Often because the real data has structure and the pipeline treats it as text.
A table row means nothing without its header; a function means nothing without
its callers; *which customers churned after the March incident* is a join
rather than a search. Chunking does not repair any of those. Give the agent a
way to query the structure — `run_sql` over a real schema, `grep` plus `read`
over a repository — instead of embedding rows and hoping.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-context-engineering-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: Why does context engineering matter if windows keep growing?**

Separate the two arguments, because they have different strengths. Cost is
close to unconditional: the transcript is re-sent on every model call, so an
uncurated context is multiplied by the step count — prompt caching discounts
an unchanged prefix but not a rewritten middle, which is why compaction is not
free — and @sec-rag measured 148× the input
tokens for identical accuracy when you skip the choosing. Capability is
conditional but documented: a claimed window is not an effective one, and
@hsieh2024ruler found half of 17 models failing to hold up at 32K, a length
all of them claim to support.

**Q: Someone shows you a perfect needle-in-a-haystack result. What do you
say?**

That it is the easy version, and say why: the needle shares a rare string with
the question, so the model matches rather than infers. Cite the contrast if you
can — @modarressi2025nolima removed the lexical overlap and 11 of 13 models
dropped below half their short-context baseline at 32K. Then give the practical
form: evaluate with paraphrases and with multi-fact aggregation, because those
are the shapes real tasks have.

**Q: What actually grows in an agent's context, and why does it cost more than
it looks?**

The transcript, monotonically — every decision and every observation is
appended and nothing is removed. It costs more than it looks because each
model call re-sends all of it, so the total is the sum of a growing series
rather than the final length — roughly quadratic in the number of sequential
steps, as @sec-agent-anatomy showed. That is why fixed costs like tool definitions
matter disproportionately: they are paid once per *call*, not once per run.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: An agent costs three times its budget. Walk me through fixing it.**

Measure by category first, and say why: the largest category is usually not
the assumed one. Then cut in order of measured cost, counting cache hits and
token prices rather than raw tokens. The usual candidates: prune tool
definitions and the system prompt, because they are multiplied by every step;
cut what tools return to the fields actually used; isolate the read-heavy sub-task into its
own context; then compact history with the facts kept verbatim. Re-measure
accuracy at every stage with an interval, because each of those can cost
points quietly.

**Q: How do you decide between eager loading and fetching on demand?**

On tokens the answer is usually "on demand", and the first-order arithmetic is
one line: eager loading costs *T* tokens on every request; just-in-time costs
the fetch tool's definition *c* on every request, plus *T* on the fraction *h*
of requests that need it. So fetching wins whenever *h* < 1 − *c*/*T*. With a
tool definition of about a hundred tokens against a two-thousand-token
document, that threshold is 0.95 — only something needed on nearly every
request is worth loading eagerly. The line leaves out one real cost: each
fetch is an extra model call, which re-sends the context so far (cheaply, if
it is cached). Say that, say what just-in-time costs in time — a round trip of
latency on the steps that need the data — and say how to get most of both:
pass identifiers rather than payloads, and dereference them only when a step
actually needs the contents.

## Lab: cut an agent's token usage without losing accuracy {#sec-context-engineering-lab}

The order of these steps matters — measure, then cut, then re-measure. Doing
it in any other order produces savings you cannot attribute. Cut first the
category that contributes most to measured cost and can be reduced safely.
That is not always the one with the most tokens: the cache-hit rate and the
token prices decide what each token costs. Steps 2–5 list the usual
candidates; if your measurement ranks them differently, follow the measurement.

### Step 1 — build the budget by category

Instrument one real run. Count tokens for: system prompt, tool definitions,
retrieved documents, tool results, conversation history. Next to each count,
record its cost, with cached and uncached input tokens priced separately. Print
the table. Do not skip to the techniques; the point of this step is that you
will be wrong about which category is largest.

### Step 2 — fix the fixed costs, if they dominate the bill

System prompt and tool definitions are re-sent on *every* call, so their
tokens are multiplied by the step count. The bill is a different matter: a
cached prefix is billed at a fraction of its first-call price
(@sec-context-engineering-cache), so check the cache-hit rate and the token
prices before putting them first. When they do dominate measured cost, this is
usually the cheapest large saving: prune tools nobody uses, and delete the
instructions that accumulated.

### Step 3 — cut what tools return

Per @sec-tool-design, return the fields the task needs rather than whole
records. Re-measure. Also check the *shape*: a 40-row result the agent only
reads two rows of should be paginated.

### Step 4 — isolate one read-heavy sub-task

Pick the step with large input and small output. Run it in its own context and
return only the conclusion. This is normally the single biggest number in the
lab.

### Step 5 — compact history, keeping facts verbatim

Summarise everything older than the last N steps, and keep a structured facts
list untouched. Sweep N over 3, 5 and 10.

### Step 6 — re-measure accuracy, not just tokens

Every step above can silently cost accuracy. Run your eval — sized per
@sec-llm-eval, because a 30-item set cannot detect the regression you care
about — and report tokens and score together. A 60% token reduction that costs
four points may or may not be worth it, but you cannot have that conversation
without both numbers.

### What to hand in

The category table before and after, the token reduction per step, the
accuracy at each stage with an interval, and one sentence on which step you
would keep if you could only keep one.

## Exercises {#sec-context-engineering-exercises}

1. **The budget table.** Instrument one real agent run and produce tokens by
   category. Write down, before you look, which category you expect to be
   largest. Most people are wrong.
2. **Multiply by steps.** Take your system prompt and tool definitions, and
   multiply their token count by the average number of model calls per run.
   That number is what pruning them is worth in tokens; if the prefix is cached,
   the saving on the bill is smaller.
3. **Paraphrase your NIAH.** If you have a long-context evaluation, rewrite
   the questions so they share no distinctive words with the answers. Re-run.
   Report both curves.
4. **Isolate one step.** Find your most read-heavy sub-task, run it in a
   separate context, and measure the parent's token count before and after.
5. **Break compaction on purpose.** Compact a transcript containing a number
   the answer needs, and check whether the number survived. Then add the
   structured facts list and check again.
6. **Hit-rate audit.** For each thing you load eagerly, measure how often it
   is actually used. Anything below about half is a candidate for
   just-in-time. (The token arithmetic in the interview questions would allow
   a much higher threshold; the extra round trip and its latency are why half
   is a sensible place to start.)
7. **Notes file.** Give an agent a scratchpad it must write findings to, and a
   tool to read sections back. Compare token usage and accuracy against the
   same agent without one, on a task long enough to need compaction.

Before reading: instrument one run and produce the token table by category. It
takes an hour and it decides which of the sections above you actually need.

| [`NoLiMa`](https://github.com/adobe-research/NoLiMa) | the needle set built without lexical overlap — the evaluation to copy rather than the vanilla one |
| [`tiktoken`](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken) | counting tokens honestly, which is step one of everything here. It implements OpenAI's tokenisers only; for other models use the model's own tokeniser or the token counts the API reports |
| [`langgraph`](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) | state as an explicit object rather than an accumulating list, which makes compaction a design decision |

## What to remember {#sec-context-engineering-summary}

- **The window is a budget, not a container.** Check both: whether the input
  fits, and whether each part earns its cost. Every token is re-sent on every
  model call, so an uncurated context is multiplied by the number of steps.
- **Count before you cut.** Tokens by category — system prompt, tool
  definitions, retrieved documents, tool results, history. The largest
  category is routinely not the assumed one. Fixed costs are paid per *call*
  rather than per run, but a cached prefix is billed at a discount, so rank
  categories by measured cost.
- **A claimed context length is a capacity, not a competence.** Of 17 models
  claiming 32K or more, only half held up at 32K [@hsieh2024ruler].
- **Needle-in-a-haystack is the easy test, and it will pass.** @sec-rag's
  retrieval run scored 100% at every position and size, and this chapter's
  60-task version stayed between 88.3% and 100% with no monotone decline — both
  with a needle that shared a rare string with the question. Remove that overlap and **11 of 13 models fall
  below half their short-context baseline at 32K**; even GPT-4o, one of the
  exceptions, goes from 99.3% to 69.7% [@modarressi2025nolima]. Evaluate with paraphrases.
- **Isolation is the largest lever *when the shape is right*.** A read-heavy
  sub-task in its own context returns a paragraph instead of forty thousand
  tokens, multiplied by every remaining call in the parent's loop.
  @sec-multi-agent modelled where it inverts: six steps producing 200-token
  results cost **1.20×** as three agents, because the per-agent fixed cost is
  paid three extra times; twenty-four steps producing 3,000-token results saved
  two thirds. Large inputs, small outputs, many remaining steps — all three, or
  it is not a saving.
- **Compaction is lossy, and you choose the loss in advance.** Keep the task
  and live tool results verbatim, summarise decisions, drop consumed results
  and resolved tracebacks — keeping a one-line lesson where it stops the same
  error recurring. Preserve exact values the answer requires.
- **Prefer identifiers to payloads.** A pointer costs ten tokens and a
  document costs two thousand, and most pointers are never dereferenced. Load
  eagerly only what is used on nearly every request.
- **When the data has structure, query the structure.** Aggregates, joins and
  exact lookups over tables are what `run_sql` over a real schema is for, and
  chunk-and-embed handles them badly; semantic search over code or prose is a
  different task, and most systems end up using the two side by side.
